21304-begumbagh-a-tale-of-the-indian-mut:
George Manville Fenn fills this volume with a long tale and three shorter stories. It starts with Begumbagh, about a small British garrison holding out during the Indian Mutiny. A one-armed narrator tells it, holding his sliding paper down with a lead inkstand. Suspense, Fenn's trademark, drives every chapter.

The second story concerns cursed gold plate in an old gentleman's house, and the curse proves real. The third traps two smugglers in a gowt, a sea drain cut in eastern England. The last follows a fine new ship through an Atlantic storm after her captain takes to drink and a junior officer takes command.
22319-mezzerow-loves-company:
Mezzerow Loves Company is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its scene opens with a welcome to Earth. An official greets newcomers arriving from the outer worlds.

He can spot fresh arrivals by one small sign. Their eyes lack the identifying gleam that marks everyone else. On principle, he would stamp one woman's passport with dull and dingy ink. That petty detail gives the future world its bureaucratic chill. The story builds its strange society out of stamps, eyes, and quiet dread. Readers meet a compact tale about belonging, papers, and being marked as an outsider on sight.
22774-barbara-in-brittany:
Barbara in Brittany is a children's story of an English girl's stay in Brittany, the Celtic corner of France. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Travel tales for girls of the era mixed mild adventure with lessons in foreign custom, and Brittany, with its pardons, costumes, and coast, was a favorite ground.

The sample catches a small moral moment: Barbara holds little Lucy in her lap and coaxes her out of shyness. You won't run off the moment she speaks to you, will you, Lucy? It's rude, you know. Try to answer nicely when she wants you to. French hosts, strange food, and new friends presumably test both girls further. The book offers a gentle tour of Brittany through a child's eyes, manners included.
brandes-main-currents-5-the-romantic-sch:
German Romantic writing fills the fifth book of Brandes's Main Currents, here in English. The Schlegels, Tieck, Novalis, and Hoffmann taught Europe new ways to dream and to doubt. Poetry, philosophy, and sly irony blend in their work.

Brandes traces how a circle of young talents remade German letters in a few bold years. He treats their longing for the infinite with sympathy and sharp insight. Fragments, fairy tales, and night pieces all find their place in his account. The volume shows why Romantic ideas from Germany spread so far across the whole of Europe.
brandes-main-currents-6-young-germany:
Young Germany closes Brandes's vast survey, in this sixth and final English book. Heine, Borne, and their allies turned writing into a weapon of politics. Literature left the study and entered the street fight for a freer Germany.

Brandes gives these radical voices his warmest praise and fullest energy. Wit, verse, and prose all serve one cause: breaking the grip of kings and censors. The survey ends where the modern age of engaged writing begins. Few works of criticism match the sweep of the full six books or their lasting sway over readers in many lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-flav: This reference piece covers Flavigny, the Burgundian abbey famed for its anise sweets. Monks have made the little candies for centuries. Henri Leclercq gives its history. A sweet-toothed corner of old France. The anise drops are still made by the old recipe today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-pont: A 1913 article on Pontigny, the Burgundian house that sheltered Becket. Exiled saints found refuge in its cloister. Edmond Obrecht tells its proud tale. Sanctuary for the persecuted. Langton hid there from King John's wrath. Its church is the purest Cistercian building in France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-savi: The Encyclopedia on Savigny, mother of a whole order. Its grey monks joined Cîteaux in time. Edmond Obrecht traces its brief glory. A reform that merged into a greater one. Its white habit passed into Cistercian use. Its daughters dotted Normandy and England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albany: This 1913 reference article on Albany — the New York diocese of the Hudson. John Walsh traces its growth. Irish immigrants built its churches. The cathedral crowns the old Dutch town. A northern see, steadily rising. Its schools serve the capital region.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-of-cl: This 1913 reference piece on Bernard of Cluny — the poet of the contempt of the world. Thomas Shahan honors his De contemptu mundi. His Hora novissima sings the heavenly city. The monks read his stern verse. The satirist of the medieval world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethany: This 1913 reference piece on Bethany — the village of Martha, Mary, and Lazarus. A.E. Breen tells its Gospel fame. Christ raised His friend from its tomb. The Mount of Olives guards its slope. The home of the Lord's friends. Its tomb church marks Lazarus' grave.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calumny: A 1913 entry on calumny — the sin of the false charge. Joseph Delany weighs its grave malice. The liar robs his neighbor's name. Restitution binds the slanderer's conscience. The sin of the lying tongue. Its reparation is the slanderer's duty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ceremony: A 1913 entry on ceremony — the sacred rite's outward form. Augustin Joseph Schulte unfolds its liturgical sense. The signs bespeak the hidden grace. The Church guards her ancient pomp. The beauty of the holy worship. Its rubrics guard the sacred action.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-huaul: A 1913 entry on Montmagny — the governor of New France. Lionel Lindsay honors his wise rule. He built the Montreal settlement. The Iroquois knew his firm hand. The Onontio of the early colony. His Sillery mission was the Jesuits' own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-: This 1913 reference piece on the Congregation of Cluny — the great Benedictine reform. George Cyprian Alston honors its thousand houses. St. Odo was its famous abbot. The order freed the monks from lay lords. The glory of the medieval monasticism. Its abbey church was the West's largest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-of-sax: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Conrad of Saxony — a Franciscan commentator of note. Stephen Donovan records his works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the order's schools. A friar among the exegetes. His Speculum is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-o-d: This 1913 reference piece on Cornelius O'Devany — the martyr Bishop of Down. The entry honors his Dublin death. He died for the persecuted flock. The faithful keep his blessed memory. A bishop among the Irish martyrs. His 1612 martyrdom is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cosmogony: This 1913 reference piece on cosmogony — the doctrine of the world's origin. John Arendzen unfolds the rival systems. Genesis crowns the revealed account. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a: This 1913 reference piece on the councils of Attigny — the Carolingian synods. Thomas Shahan notes their ancient acts. The bishops met in the royal palace. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epiphany: This 1913 reference article on the Epiphany — the Magi's feast. Cyril Charles Martindale unfolds its joyful rite. The kings bore the mystic gifts. The waters of Jordan hallowed the day. The manifestation of the newborn King. Its January sixth is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-bauny: A 1913 entry on Étienne Bauny — the Jesuit casuist. Timothy Barrett notes his famous Somme. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the moral schools. A doctor of the seventeenth century. His 1640 Somme is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-joseph-: This 1913 reference article on Franz Joseph Antony — the German composer. James Völker notes his famous works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the nineteenth century. A musician among the clergy. His 1837 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-germany: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Germany — the empire's Catholic story. Kampers and Spahn trace the ancient faith. Boniface planted the German Church. The Reformation rent the father's house. The Kulturkampf tested the loyal sons. Its 496 baptism is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gluttony: This 1913 reference piece on gluttony — the table's vice. Joseph Delany unfolds its moral kinds. The belly rules the reason's throne. The fast curbs the unruly appetite. The capital sin of the intemperate feast. Its seven sins are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-harmony: A 1913 entry on harmony — the concord of sounds. Joseph Otten unfolds its musical laws. The voices blend the sweet accord. The schools weigh the subtle art. The science of the chorded tones. Its counterpoint is famed.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-litany: This 1913 reference article on the Litany — the responsive prayer. Francis Mershman unfolds its liturgical lore. The people answer the priest's plea. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludolph-of-sa: A 1913 entry on Ludolph — the Carthusian mystic. Ambrose Mougel honors his Vita Christi. His pen pictured the Savior's life. The order prized its holy son. The fourteenth century knew his name. His 1378 death is famed. His 1374 Vita is famed. His 1374 Christ's life is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orders-of-sai: This entry surveys the orders and congregations under St. Anthony's patronage, from the hospitallers of the Middle Ages to the modern congregations, tracing their foundations and works as the 1913 editors recorded them. The many families of the wonder-worker: their hospitals served the sick for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pardons-of-br: The Pardons are Brittany's great pilgrimages, when parishes process to the shrines in traditional costume. This entry describes their history, their rites, and their fervor. The faith of the Bretons, on the march: their colorful banners fill the country roads.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-pazmany: Cardinal Pázmány was the Jesuit who won Hungary back to the Catholic faith. This entry traces his career, his writings, and his triumphs. The apostle of Hungary: his famous university at Nagyszombat lives on in the schools of modern Budapest today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saxony: Saxony became the kingdom of the Elbe valley. This long entry covers its electors, its Catholics, and its history. The faith of the Dresden land: its great churches serve the kingdom in Dresden's city in the Elbe's valley in the east.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scrutiny: Scrutiny is the examination of the candidate. This entry explains its kinds, its law, and its use. The testing of the ordinand: its searching questions prove the candidate in the 1900s' Church in the dioceses of the world in the Code.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sejny: Sejny became the diocese of Poland's Suwałki region. This entry covers its bishops, its churches, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the Lithuanian border: its old churches serve Sejny in Poland's northeast in the lakes of the region.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simony: Simony is the buying of the sacred. This long entry examines its kinds, its penalties, and its history. The sin of the Gehazi bargain: its stern penalties bind the clergy in the 1900s' Code in the canons of the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anthony: St. Anthony was the father of the monks. This long entry examines his desert, his temptations, and his fame. The hermit of the Egyptian Thebaid: his lonely desert crowned the monks in the 270s' Thebaid in the south of Egypt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lazarus-of: St. Lazarus was the friend raised from the dead. This long entry examines his Bethany, his sisters, and his cult. The brother of the Gospel household: his empty tomb crowned Bethany in the Gospels of the Church in the lectionary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vitalis-of: St. Vitalis of Savigny was the founder hermit. This entry traces his Savigny, his rule, and his fame. The abbot of the Norman forest: his new order crowned Savigny in the 1110s' Normandy in the forest of the Fougères in France.
charter-and-supplemental-charter-of-the-: This volume prints the founding legal documents of the Hudson's Bay Company — the 1670 royal charter from Charles II granting it vast trading rights over northern North America. These few pages of legal language shaped the history of Canada, opening the fur trade that drew Europeans deep into the continent. Essential reading for understanding how Canada began.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ImperialeAnthon: A United Press International item reports that Anthony Imperiale, described in the headline as a New Jersey white militant, sought a coalition of American rightists. Imperiale was a Newark figure who built his name on street patrols and hard-right politics. The surviving record gives the wire service and the headline claim but no date, so the piece stands as a UPI report on his organizing effort.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MarshWAnthony_M: W. Anthony Marsh wrote this rebuttal in August 1983, answering Ramsey, the head of the National Academy of Sciences committee on ballistic acoustics. That committee had reviewed the acoustics evidence in the Kennedy case and rejected the finding of a likely second gunman. Marsh, an independent researcher, disputes the committee's work point by point. The file gives his title and position, but not the rebuttal's detailed arguments.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va: Joint Task Force ARES was the United States Cyber Command unit built to fight the Islamic State online, and Operation GLOWING SYMPHONY was its main campaign. This Cyber Vault page presents the record of that internet war against ISIL. A companion Archive release covers Cyber Command's own after-action assessments of the same operation. The evidence here is the title alone, so this page works best as the overview entry, with the assessment documents supplying the graded details.
kenny:
Kenny is a novel by Leona Dalrymple, issued by Reilly and Britton, with a second printing in September 1917. Joseph Pierre Nuyttens illustrated it. Twenty-two chapters run from Brian Rebels to A Chronicle Concluded. The early titles name Kenny himself as the unsuccessful parent of his son Brian.

Joan enters in chapter three, and Adam Craig blackmails somebody in chapter four. A cabin in the pines, Kenny's truth crusade, and Samhain Night give the middle its color. Kenny finds the rainbow's end, becomes himself again, and faces a shadow of death. Dalrymple writes of an artist father whose charm and selfishness his son must outgrow. The Irish names and feast days flavor this family romance.
letters-of-pliny:
Pliny the Younger's letters offer a polished picture of Roman life. An introduction notes he was born at Como in 62 AD. His father died when Pliny was eight years old.

His uncle, Pliny the Elder, adopted and raised him. The elder Pliny wrote the famous Natural History. Young Pliny studied rhetoric under Quintilian and other noted teachers. He became the most eloquent pleader of his time, the introduction says. He also served as a military tribune in Syria. His letters imitate Cicero's style with care and pride. His account of Vesuvius erupting survives among these letters. That report remains the volcano's classic eyewitness record.
malvina-of-brittany:
Malvina of Brittany is a story collection by Jerome K. Jerome, headed by its title tale. A doctor narrates the preface and swears he never believed the story. Yet he claims it altered his whole outlook on life. Cousin Christopher gets mixed up in Malvina's strange affair.

Malvina is a lovely Breton girl with something of the fey about her. Love crosses the border of legend in her tale. Other stories here include 'The Street of the Blank Wall' and 'The Fawn Gloves.' Jerome writes in his mellowest, dreamiest mood. The book mixes Celtic twilight with his usual gentle humor. It shows a softer side of the Three Men in a Boat author.
my-four-years-in-germany:
James W. Gerard, America's envoy to Germany, tells of four hard years. He served at the Kaiser's imperial court until 1917. His foreword warns that Germany's power stands unbroken. He gives stark counts of men called, killed, and held.

Gerard says Americans do not grasp the war's vast scale. Five million prisoners are held across all lands, he notes. Pictures show court balls and his safe conduct home. The book was a wartime sensation when it appeared. It gives the view from the embassy as peace broke, talks failed, and America moved toward war.
over-strand-and-field-a-record-of-travel:
Gustave Flaubert traveled through Brittany as a young man. His friend Maxime Du Camp went with him. Over Strand and Field is the record, published in English at Chicago in 1904. Its first chapter is not Brittany at all. It is the Château de Chambord. The travelers walk empty galleries there. Spiders spin cobwebs over the salamanders of Francis the First.

Flaubert finds the château's poverty conscious and sad. It brushes its threadbare coat and tries to look respectable. One floor is repaired while the next rots. He retells its parade of owners. Gaston d'Orléans was exiled there. Louis the Fourteenth ruined the double staircase. Molière first staged Le Bourgeois gentilhomme under its crumbling ceilings. The young Flaubert already sees like the novelist he became.
podcast-dannyjones-q3i8X03minY:
Guitarist Vernon Reid, founder of the band Living Colour, warns Danny Jones that AI music tools like AI Drake are becoming a real problem. Fake songs in the voices of famous artists flooded the internet, and Reid sees danger for real musicians. The talk is about machines mimicking souls, as Reid puts it.

Reid explains what is lost when a program copies a singer's style without living the life behind it. He and Jones discuss credit, pay, and who owns a voice. They also ask what live playing still offers that code cannot. Musicians and fans get an artist's clear-eyed warning on fake art.
podcast-joerogan-fcdItgUjZnY:
Joe Rogan asks what goes on in the brain in a DMT trip in a segment from his show. DMT is the drug that fires a full dream world in mere minutes. Rogan is the show world's best known fan of the drug.

Rogan works through what scans and reports say the brain does at the peak of the trip. He weighs the view that the mind opens a door from the view that it just misfires in style. The segment is short and dense. Listeners get the science side of his pet topic. The library holds the file as an archive record.
richard-of-jamestown-a-story-of-the-virg: James Otis — the beloved author of Toby Tyler — tells the story of Richard of Jamestown and the Virginia colony's hard founding years. Hunger, Indians, and Captain John Smith fill this stirring tale for boys. American history made thrilling for young readers, who will cheer Richard's courage.
roads-of-destiny: O. Henry's 1909 story collection, named for the title tale of three roads a shepherd might take. More twists, more New York and Western color, more warmth. Published the year before his death, it shows his gift undimmed.
samuel-brohl-and-company: Victor Cherbuliez's novel about Samuel Brohl and Company: a scoundrel's schemes in European society. Clever and satirical, it was a great French success. A fine novel of manners and roguery. Cherbuliez's rogue is as charming as he is wicked.
tacitus-on-germany: Tacitus's Germania: the Roman's portrait of the German tribes. The classic that shaped Germany's self-image. Ancient ethnography at its finest. Rome's view of the German tribes, the classic Germania, ancient ethnography at its finest.
the-curlytops-at-uncle-frank-s-ranch-or-: Howard Garis — creator of Uncle Wiggily — sends the Curlytops to Uncle Frank's ranch for ponyback adventures. The cheerful twins find fun, mild scrapes, and new friends among cowboys and cattle. Wholesome, old-fashioned children's entertainment from a master of the genre.
the-house-of-dust-a-symphony: Conrad Aiken's 1920 modernist poem-sequence: a series of meditations on love, death, and illusion, spoken by the dead in a "house of dust." Influenced by Eliot and Freud, it is dreamlike, musical, and haunting. A landmark of early American modernism, strange and beautiful.
the-white-company: Arthur Conan Doyle's 1891 medieval adventure, his favorite among his own books. Young Alleyne leaves his monastery to join the White Company of English archers fighting in France, in a tale of chivalry, battles, and comradeship. Researched with care and told with gusto, it is historical fiction of the first rank.
through-five-republics-on-horseback-bein: George Whitfield Ray rode on horseback through five South American republics, and this is the account of his many wanderings. Part missionary, part explorer, he crossed mountains and jungles few travelers had seen. His narrative blends high adventure with deep Christian faith. Strange peoples, wild lands, and constant peril fill the pages. A remarkable record of travel in a little-known continent.
